question: Many professionals in the business of repairing and analysing electric personal transport vehicles are expressing concern about the appearance on the EU market of e-scooters and components that present significant safety risks and often come with CE certifications that are fraudulent or have no legal standing.

Technical reports point to electrical faults during normal use of light electric vehicles (LEVs) containing high-power lithium batteries. These faults arise from a lack of basic protection features, such as means to limit current or enable automatic shut-off. Owing to these shortcomings, LEVs pose a fire and thermal runaway hazard and also distort competition at the expense of stakeholders who comply with EU rules.

LEVs are sold through large online sales platforms operating in the EU and despite warnings that they may be dangerous, are not recalled or issued with safety alerts, calling into question the effectiveness of market surveillance. In view of the above, can the Commission clarify: 1.
how it assesses the application and effectiveness of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 in the case of electric personal transport vehicles sold online?
what measures it is considering to improve the safety of batteries and electric micromobility systems?
how it intends to make importers and marketplaces more accountable, and whether it is considering targeted action or intending to strengthen the regulatory framework specific to batteries?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.3.2026) There is currently no harmonised EU legislation governing the on-road safety of electric micromobility products, except for speed pedelecs1. These products fall under the Machinery Directive2, covering i.a. battery safety, while enforcement is carried out by the national market surveillance authorities.

Where products are not covered by harmonised legislation, the General Product Safety Regulation (GPSR)3 requires those products placed on the EU market to be safe. Manufacturers bear the main responsibility for product’s safety. Under the GPSR, the Commission may take EU action against products posing a serious risk, including by prohibiting or restricting their sale or imposing testing or marketing conditions.

Ensuring product compliance, notably for goods sold online and imported from third countries, remains a major Single Market challenge, as highlighted in the Single Market Strategy and the e-commerce communication. To address this, the Commission has announced a revision of the Market Surveillance Regulation4, as part of the European Product Act (EPA), also covering standardisation and conformity assessment.
It aims to close regulatory loopholes in e-commerce, strengthen digital tools, enhance cooperation and pool resources.

At the same time, the revision of the Union Customs Code5 will reinforce enforcement, including by making online suppliers or platforms responsible for the financial and non-financial obligations related to the products they sell, through the ‘deemed importer’ concept, and EU-level tools such as the EU Customs Data Hub and the EU Customs Authority.
